title: Rapid Increase in Geogenic CO2 Emissions from Antarctic Permafrost
content:
Abstract

Thawing permafrost can amplify climate change by releasing previously stored carbon, but observations of this feedback come mainly from the Arctic. Ice-free Antarctic terrains are generally regarded as minor CO2 sources, although sub-permafrost brines and deep carbon reservoirs may support localized geogenic degassing. We report repeated soil CO2 flux and soil-gas surveys in the Taylor Valley in 2020, 2023, and 2025. The mean flux increased from 1.73 to 9.49 g CO2 m−2 d−1, the median from 1.20 to 6.70 g CO2 m−2 d−1, the 90th percentile from 4.11 to 20.62 g CO2 m−2 d−1, and the maximum from 11.36 to 72.99 g CO2 m−2 d−1. Carbon isotope ratios of CO2 and CH4 are consistent with a substantial deep geogenic contribution and thermogenic or mixed signatures, with limited microbial influence at the highest flux sites. Geological and electrical-resistivity observations identify heterogeneous permafrost, brine-bearing horizons, and potential permeable pathways, but the available data do not establish whether permafrost thaw or subglacial drainage caused the temporal increase. Conditional scaling of the campaign-specific areal emission densities to the 4,500 km2 ice-free area of the McMurdo Dry Valleys yields 1.14–15.90 Mt CO2 yr−1, whereas scaling to 21,745 km2 of mapped Antarctic ice-free terrain yields 5.51–76.84 Mt CO2 yr−1, equivalent to a maximum of approximately 0.021 Pg C yr−1. These calculations represent illustrative spatial-scaling scenarios rather than regional emission inventories or temporal forecasts. The observations demonstrate substantial, spatially focused geogenic degassing and motivate co-located thermal, hydrological, and geophysical monitoring.
